text: ECE 60146 HW2 Andrea Goh January 2025 1 Introduction The goal of this assignment is to gain familiarity with image representations provided by the PIL, Numpy, and PyTorch libraries. This assignment will also explore the concept of data augmentation. Additionally, in this assignment, we will be introduced to the essential components for building an image dataloader to train or test deep neural networks. 2 Pixel Value Scaling, Normalization and Data Augmentation 2.1 Pixel Value Scaling and Normalization Image data consists of integers ranging from 0 to 255. However, neural networks prefer input data to be floating-point numbers ranging from -1.0 to 1.0. To meet this requirement, pixel value scaling is first used to map the integer image data (0 to 255) to the floating-point range (0, 1.0). Then, pixel value normalization is used to map the scaled pixel values to
title: PyTorch Datasets & DataLoaders

text: integer image data (0 to 255) to the floating-point range (0, 1.0). Then, pixel value normalization is used to map the scaled pixel values to span the floating-point range (-1.0, 1.0). The normalization step is particularly important for neural networks because it centers the data around zero, which can improve the convergence behavior during training. 2.2 Data Augmentation In this assignment, the custom dataset that we create starts with 20 base images. These 20 images are augmented to obtain a total of 50 image samples. These augmentations will include random rotations, flips, cropping, and color adjustments. The purpose of data augmentation is to introduce variability within the training dataset, which can reduce overfitting and improve generalization. 2.3 Transformations Pixel value scaling, normalization and data augmentation can be implemented using the torchvi- sion.transforms module. The transformation pipeline used in this assignment

Normalize ((0.5 ,0.5 ,0.5) ,(0.5 ,0.5 ,0.5)) ]) Using the code above, the custom dataset can be generated by applying random flips, rotation, and crop to the base image. The transforms.ToTensor() transformation applies pixel value scaling. transforms.Normalize((0.5,0.5,0.5),(0.5,0.5,0.5)) applies pixel value normalization, where the first arg, (0.5,0.5,0.5), is subtracted from the corresponding channel pixel value and the result is then divided by the second arg, (0.5,0.5,0.5). The convergence is also more unstable with the higher learning rate. 1.3 SGD with Momentum (SGD+) GD and SGD run into the same problem when the cost-function surface is a narrow valley, as opposed to a round valley. If the same learning rate is used for all iterations, after reaching the bottom of the valley, while the direction of movement is toward the optimum point, due to the learning rate, the solution path will crisscross the ravine. The problem with this is that we may never get a good sense of whether we are sufficiently close to the goal. One solution to this problem is to apply momentum in step-size calculations for learnable parameter values, and biases. Let: • wt: model parameters at time step t • gt = ∇L(wt): gradient of the loss function
title: Backpropagation & Optimizers, From Scratch

text: calculations for learnable parameter values, and biases. Let: • wt: model parameters at time step t • gt = ∇L(wt): gradient of the loss function L at step t • vt: velocity (accumulated gradient) 2

text: • η: learning rate • β: momentum coefficient The basic update rule for SGD follows the equation: wt+1 = wt − ηgt, where ηgt+1 represents the change in the solution path at time step t. Momentum involves carrying forward a portion of the previous update to influence the current step. These updates are computed as: vt+1 = βvt + gt (1) wt+1 = wt − ηvt+1 (2) The way momentum works is that if the previous step is in the same direction as the current step, we go downhill quicker by increasing the step size. On the other hand, if the previous step is in the opposite direction as the current, we know that the optimum point was passed, and hence, the step size is reduced. This method helps navigate ravines more effectively by reducing oscillations and improving optimization stability.

This method helps navigate ravines more effectively by reducing oscillations and improving optimization stability. 1.3.1 Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) Adam estimates on a running-average basis the first and second momentum, denoted as mt and vt respectively: mt = β1 ∗ mt−1 + (1 − β1) ∗ gradt (3) vt+1 = β2 ∗ vt + (1 − β2) ∗ (gradt)2 (4) Typically, the constant values for β1 and β2 are close to 1. The recursion is also initialized such that m0 = v0 = 0. However, this zero initialization results in a bias towards zero for the two momentum for several training iterations. When the learning rate is 0.001, SGD converges with a much higher loss value compared to SGD+ and Adam. text: and Normalization Image data consists of integers ranging from 0 to 255. However, neural networks prefer input data to be floating-point numbers ranging from -1.0 to 1.0. To meet this requirement, pixel value scaling is first used to map the integer image data (0 to 255) to the floating-point range (0, 1.0). Then, pixel value normalization is used to map the scaled pixel values to span the floating-point range (-1.0, 1.0). 3.2 Comparing Performance with and without data normalization In this section, we compare the performance between models that normalize data and models that dont. text: ECE 60146 HW 04 Andrea Goh (goh8@purdue.edu) February 2025 1 Introduction The goal of this assignment is to assess how classification accuracy is influenced by object quantity, diversity, and whether the object is the primary focus of the image. To do so, we begin by creating three different dataset variants. The same CNN model will be trained on each of the datasets variants and classification accuracy for each will be analyzed. The three datasets created will be as follows: 1. Single-instance dataset: Images containing only one instance of an object. 2. Multi-instance (same object) dataset: Images containing multiple instances of the same object. 3. Multi-instance (different objects) dataset: Images containing multiple objects from different cate- gories. 2 Programming Tasks 2.1 Create Image Classification Dataset 1 2 from pycocotools . coco import COCO 3 import os 4 from PIL import Image

text: 2.2.2 Results Figure 7: Training Loss for all Datasets Dataset Single Instance Multi Instance Same Multi Instance Diff Accuracy 56.09% 53.98% 46.31% Table 3: Accuracy Out of all the datasets, the CNN performed best on the single instance dataset, and worst on the different multi-instance dataset. These results make sense because we would expect classification to become more difficult when three are multiple objects in an image, and even more difficult when those multiple object are different. The labels on the confusion matrices represent the following classes: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] = [’airplane’, ’bird’, ’giraffe’, ’clock’, ’zebra’]. From the confusion matrices, we can see that images of zebras were commonly misclassified as giraffes. This is true across all datasets, and especially for the multi-instance same dataset. This makes sense because both zebras and giraffes are animals that walk on
title: Custom CNN Classifier & Dataset Design

text: is true across all datasets, and especially for the multi-instance same dataset. This makes sense because both zebras and giraffes are animals that walk on four legs. The differentiating factor between zebras and giraffes could be the stripes that zebras have. However, our dataset contains downsized 64 ×64 images. Thus, whenever there are multiple of zebras captured in an image, it is likely that the resolution of those zebras are low and thus, the stripes are not captured in those images. An example of a zebra that was misclassified as a giraffe is shown in figure 11. The zebras in the photo are of such low resolution that their stripes are not discernible. text: ECE 60146 HW 06 Andrea Goh February 2025 1 Playing with Skip Connections 1.1 Task 1: Comparing the use of a1 × 1 Kernel On page 16 of week 6 lecture, the definition for SkipBlock contain convolutional operators that uses 1×1 kernel. Convolutions that are carried out with a 1 pixel kernel, is essentially a scaling operator. Each pixel in the input image is multiplied by the kernel value to generate the output pixel. The purpose SkipBlock uses such a convolution is for two reasons, to change the number of channels, and to downsample the image. In line (I) of the SkipBlock definition code, the convolution looks like:self.in2out = nn.Conv2d(inch, out ch, 1). This convolution has a 1 pixel kernel and a stride of 1, which is default. Since the stride is 1, each pixel in each of the in
title: CNN Architecture Ablations: Skip Connections

text: has a 1 pixel kernel and a stride of 1, which is default. Since the stride is 1, each pixel in each of the in ch channels of the input image is multiplied by the kernel pixel value to obtain each of the out ch channels. Thus, the purpose of this line is to change the number of channels from in ch to out ch. In line (K) and (L), the convolution looks like: self.downsampler1 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, 1, stride=2) and self.downsampler1 = nn.Conv2d(outch, outch, 1, stride=2). This convolution has a 1 pixel kernel and a stride of 2. In this case, the number of input channels and output channels remain the same. However, the stride of 2 means that every other pixel in the input image is being multiplied by the kernel value to obtain the output image. Therefore,
title: CNN Architecture Ablations: Skip Connections

text: stride of 2 means that every other pixel in the input image is being multiplied by the kernel value to obtain the output image. Therefore, the purpose of this 1 pixel convolution is to downsize the size of the image by half. 2 Comparing two Methods for Downsizing In this section, we will be comparing two different methods for downsizing. Net1 uses a stride length of 2 with a kernel size of 1 to perform downsizing. This means it does not aggregate the information from neighboring pixels. Rather, it downsizes by skipping every other pixel. On the other hand, Net2 uses MaxPool2d(2,2), which essentially selects the maximum value within each 2×2 patch. Thus, it preserves the most dominant features. Figure 1: Running Loss Comparison 1

The displacement from the bounding box center to the center of that cell is calculated (δx and δy). Finally, an anchor box is selected based on the aspect ratio of the bounding box. Then, the yolo vector is constructed: [1 , δx, δy, h, w,1, 0, 0], where 1 indicates the presence of a bounding box, h and w represent the height and width of the bounding box normalized by the image dimensions, and the last three elements correspond to the one-hot encoding of the object class. From the indices, the x and y grid can be found. From the yolo vector, the displacements of the center of the bbox to the center of the grid cell can be extracted (x diff, y diff). Then, the center of the bounding box can be calculated using the grid center coordinates and the displacement coordinates. Next, the height and width of the bbox is extracted from the yolo vector. text: ECE 60146 HW 08 Andrea Goh March 2025 1 mUnet The output of mUnet is a mask corresponding to the input images. In the PurdueShapes5 dataset, these masks consist of five channels, each representing one of the five object classes: rectangle, triangle, disk, oval, and star. mUnet follows an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder extracts object features by progressively reducing the spatial dimensions of the input image, allowing it to capture high-level representations. The decoder then reconstructs the spatial information by gradually upsampling the feature maps generated by the encoder. Skip connections transfers information between the encoder and decoder, helping to preserve pixel-level details, which improves decoder’s performance. 2 Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) 2.1 Code Implementation 1 class mUNet (nn. The same misclassifications occurs when the MSE and dice losses are combined with the same scale. However, when the MSE and dice loss are combined at a scale of 1 and 5, the oval that was previously classified as a rectangle becomes correctly classified. When the scale on the dice loss is further increased to 10, one of the ovals again gets misclassified as a rectangle. Therefore, the best ratio between MSE and dice loss to use for the combined loss function is 1:5. text: ECE 60146 HW09 Andrea Goh March 2025 1 Generative Adversarial Nets (GAN) 1.1 Theory In this assignment, a Discriminator-Generator based Adversarial Network is used. This type of generative model is estimated via an adversarial process, which simultaneously trains a generative model G, and a discriminative model D. The goal of the generative model is to capture the data distribution, while the goal of the discriminative model is to estimate the probability that the sample came from the training data rather than G. 1.2 The Discriminator Network The discriminator network in this section was copied directly from Professor Kak’s AdversarialLearn- ing.py. This discriminator network is also known as the 4-2-1 network because the first four convolutions are carried out with a kernel size of 4, stride length of 2, and padding of 1. The first four layers of the network begin

text: 1.3 The Generator Network The generator network in this section was copied directly from Professor Kak’s AdversarialLearn- ing.py. The input to the generator network is a noise vector, which is a 1x1 image with 100 channels. The input to the network is first passed through a transpose convolution withe a kernel size of 4, stride length of 1, and padding size of 0. Then, the next four layers follows the same structure: batch normal- ization → ReLU → Transpose Convolution. The transpose convolution in these four layers follow the 4-2-1 structure, where the kernel size is 4, stride length is 2, and padding is 1. Finally, the output is then passed through a Tanh activation function to generate the final output of the network, which will be the generated fake image with three channels. 1 # ####################### Start : Copied
